title: Aad sach: the sound
hook: aad sach, jugaad sach, hai bhi sach, Nanak hosi bhi sach

segments.voice: Yesterday, jap, the one-word title: recite, repeat, remember. Your line was repeat, remember. What did you repeat three times on purpose? Day one hundred sixty-one.

Right after the title, jap, comes a short verse, a salok, just two lines long. It's one of the most sung lines in the Sikh world. You'll hear it at the start of Japji every morning, and you'll hear it at gatherings as kirtan, sung round and round until the whole room is singing. It has a shape you can feel before you know a single word: four little claims, with the same word landing at the end of each one. Like a drum hitting the same beat four times.
screen: `A SALOK, TWO LINES LONG.` → `SUNG ROUND AND ROUND.` → `ONE WORD, FOUR TIMES.`

segments.voice: Here it is, slowly. Aad sach. Jugaad sach. Hai bhee sach. Naanak hosee bhee sach. Listen for the word that keeps coming back: sach. It sounds a little like such, said softly. That's the drumbeat. Now the pieces. Aad: a long a, as in father. Jugaad: ju-GAAD, and inside it is the word jug, an age, a great stretch of time. Hai bhee: hai, like high, and bhee, like bee with a breath on the b. Naanak: the Guru's own name, NAA-nak. Hosee bhee: HO-see bhee. Now notice the shape. The first line is two short pairs: aad sach, jugaad sach. The second line stretches out: three beats, then four. As if the verse leans forward. And listen to what the pieces sound like even before you know them: aad, a beginning; jug, the ages; hai, is; hosee, will be. It moves from before, through the long ages, to right now, and on into what's coming. And in every line, the same word holds still while the time around it moves. The sound is already doing the teaching before the meaning arrives. Tomorrow we'll open what sach means and what the four lines claim. Today it's enough to hear one word holding the whole verse up. In Gurmukhi, sach carries the same small silent mark under its last letter that you saw on jap. Many sangats sing this salok as simple kirtan, and it's one of the easiest to join.
screen: `SACH — THE DRUMBEAT.` · `AAD, JUGAAD, HAI BHEE, HOSEE.` · `THE SECOND LINE STRETCHES.` · `ONE WORD HOLDS STILL.` · then, large: `AAD SACH.`

segments.voice: Say it four times, out loud if you can. Aad sach. Jugaad sach. Hai bhee sach. Naanak hosee bhee sach. Again, a little slower, letting sach land each time. Again, softer. And once more, almost a whisper. Then sit, and let the last sach fade. Notice that your breath went on the whole time, underneath the words. If you pray, you can stay with Waheguru in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
screen: `ਆਦਿ ਸਚੁ ਜੁਗਾਦਿ ਸਚੁ ॥ ਹੈ ਭੀ ਸਚੁ ਨਾਨਕ ਹੋਸੀ ਭੀ ਸਚੁ ॥`

segments.voice: Aad sach. The opening words of the salok after the Mool Mantar. One word, sach, holds the whole verse up.

Your line: aad sach. Say it once as you wake tomorrow. And look back at this week: a shield for others, your rhythm, the Guru's alphabet, sound before meaning, the Mool Mantar, and jap. Day one hundred sixty-one.

howItsDone: The salok 'aad sach, jugaad sach' follows the Mool Mantar at the start of Japji; sangats also sing it as simple kirtan, repeating it many times.

fork.setup: you're hearing the salok for the first time. which word keeps coming back?

original.note: Gurmukhi: the salok after the Mool Mantar, Ang 1.

trapdoor: what it means: a two-line salok in which one word, sach, lands four times across past, ages, now and future.
what a scholar hears: jugaad joins jug, an age, to aad, beginning; the verse also closes the Mool Mantar for those who read it as longer.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1 (salok after the Mool Mantar)

notes: Jugaad as jug + aad (beginning of the ages): common gloss; confirm.
